newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel-Palestinian violence flares after bombing.
newsitem.headline: Israel-Palestinian violence flares after bombing.

text.p: Fierce clashes flared along an Israeli-Palestinian confrontation line in the West Bank town of Hebron on Saturday, putting more strain on the Middle East peace process a day after an Arab suicide bombing in Tel Aviv.

Palestinian security forces in Gaza rearrested a recently freed leader of the Islamic group Hamas that claimed responsibility for the Tel Aviv cafe attack that killed three Israeli women, a Hamas source said.

In fresh violence, hundreds of Palestinian youths shouting "Allahu Akbar" (God is Greatest) threw petrol bombs and rocks at Israeli soldiers who responded with rubber bullets and teargas in the West Bank town of Hebron.
Hospital officials said at least 20 Arab protesters were wounded by rubber bullets and one demonstrator lost an eye.
The clashes followed similar violence in Hebron on Friday along a rock-strewn confrontation line dividing the Israeli- and Palestinian-controlled parts of the city.

"Tension is very high because of (Israeli leader Benjamin) Netanyahu's crazy policy," said Palestinian West Bank security chief Jibril Rajoub, whose arrival in Hebron with police reinforcements quelled the violence only briefly.
He was referring to the groundbreaking last Tuesday for a Jewish settlement at Jabal Abu Ghenim, or Har Homa, in Arab East Jerusalem.
The internationally condemned plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews would add another link to an Israeli chain of apartment blocks cutting off East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank.
In Gaza, a Hamas source who declined to be identified said Ibrahim al-Makadmeh, a leader of a military wing of the group, was taken into custody late on Friday.

Makadmeh, who Palestinian President Yasser Arafat released from jail this week, told a rally on Friday after the suicide attack during the Jewish costume holiday of Purim that only bombs could stop Israel's settlement drive.

Netanyahu had accused Arafat of tacitly giving Hamas a "green light" to strike against the Jewish state by freeing Makadmeh and other militants arrested last year after suicide bombers killed 59 people in Israel.
The attack was a political embarrassment for Netanyahu who won election last May promising more security for Israelis.

Israeli Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani rejected Palestinian suggestions that the decision to push ahead with the construction in East Jerusalem meant Israel had brought the bombing upon itself.

"A year ago there was a prime minister who was the best one for the Arabs -- Shimon Peres -- and they attacked us," he told Army Radio, referring to Hamas. "There were explosions everywhere even though we were not building at Har Homa."
A Hamas official who asked not to be identified said Friday's bombing might not be the last.
"If Israeli policy continues in the same direction, I think that yesterday's operation will not be the last," the official said.
Arafat condemned the blast, which also wounded 42 people, and telephoned Netanyahu to express condolences.

Israel clamped a closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip and sealed the home of the suicide bomber, identified by Palestinian sources as Mousa Abdel-Qader Ghneimat, 28, from the Israeli-controlled West Bank village of Sourif.
The army said it had arrested 13 Sourif residents and four people from the village of Nuva in the Hebron area as part of the investigation of the Tel Aviv bombing.
